title: Values, Names and Variables
learningObjectives: Define a value as data a program can use, including numbers, text strings, and true/false Boolean values.
Explain how values represent information used in calculations, decisions, messages, comparisons, and other program operations.
Distinguish a value from the name used to refer to it, using examples such as 25 and studentAge.
Define a name as a label that identifies a program element and explain why descriptive names improve readability.
Explain a variable as a named binding through which code refers to a value, rather than treating it only as a physical box.
Identify the declaration keyword, identifier, assignment operator, and value in a JavaScript variable declaration.
Explain that a variable name is an identifier and recognize identifiers in short code examples.
Apply JavaScript naming rules: identifiers cannot begin with a digit, contain spaces, or use reserved keywords.
Explain case sensitivity and distinguish identifiers such as score and Score.
Choose meaningful names such as studentName, totalPrice, and itemCount instead of unclear names.
Use const for a binding that should not be reassigned and explain the restriction it creates.
Use let for a binding that may need a new value and demonstrate reassignment.
Distinguish reassignment of a const binding from changing properties or elements of an object or array it refers to.
Predict the values displayed after a sequence of variable declarations and assignments.
Identify naming mistakes such as leading digits, spaces, reserved words, and inconsistent capitalization.
Correct a simple declaration by choosing a valid identifier and suitable declaration keyword.
Explain how purposeful names make code easier to read, maintain, review, and debug.
Create a JavaScript example that stores related information in separate variables and displays it.
Trace how a value is associated with a variable name and then used in a later expression or statement.
Connect values, names, identifiers, and variables to later topics such as data types, operators, expressions, conditions, loops, and functions.

understand.concept: A value is data a program can use, such as 25, "Ravi", true, or false. A name identifies a program element. A variable is a named binding through which code refers to a value. In JavaScript, variables are commonly declared with const or let; the variable name is an identifier.
understand.whyItMatters: Programs need data to calculate, decide, display messages, and compare information. Values provide the data; names explain what it represents; variables let code refer to it repeatedly. Clear names reduce confusion and make code easier to read, maintain, and debug.
understand.history: This lesson focuses on transferable programming concepts; detailed language history is taught in the relevant language module.
understand.analogy: A library catalogue uses a book's title or catalogue entry to identify it. In a similar way, a program uses a name to refer to a value. The name is not the data itself; it helps code identify the data it needs.
understand.analogyLimit: A variable is not always a physical box in memory. In JavaScript, it is more accurate to think of it as a binding between a name and a value. const prevents reassignment of the binding, but it does not automatically make an object or array deeply immutable.

explain.narrative: A value is the actual data used by a program. For example, 25 is a Number, "Ravi" is a String, and true is a Boolean value. A name communicates the purpose of the information: studentName is clearer than x. In JavaScript, a variable name is an identifier. It cannot begin with a digit, contain spaces, or use a reserved keyword. JavaScript is case-sensitive, so score and Score are different identifiers.\n\nIn `const studentName = "Ravi";`, const is the declaration keyword, studentName is the identifier, = is the assignment operator, and "Ravi" is the value. Use const when the binding should not be reassigned and let when it needs a new value later. const prevents reassignment of the binding; it does not automatically freeze the contents of an object or array.

examples.explanation: The example stores a String, a Number, and a Boolean value in descriptive variables. Each name communicates the purpose of its value.
shopName uses const because its binding is not reassigned. totalItems uses let and is reassigned from 10 to 15.
The first three identifiers are valid. An identifier cannot start with a digit or contain a space.
examples.expectedOutput: The first three declarations are valid; the commented examples are invalid.

practise.guidedTask: For each declaration, identify the keyword, variable name, and value. Classify each value as a String, Number, or Boolean. Explain how the name communicates the purpose of the data.
practise.independentTask: Write a JavaScript program that stores a shop name, product name, price, quantity, and stock status. Use const for bindings that should not be reassigned and let for a value that changes. Display the information and explain your choices.
hints: Identify the actual data value first, then choose a name that explains its purpose.
Use readable camelCase names such as productName and totalPrice.
Do not start an identifier with a digit or include spaces.
Use const when the binding will not be reassigned and let when it needs a new value.
const prevents reassignment of the binding; it does not automatically freeze an object or array.
